newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Chechen warlords invoke Islam in presidential race.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chechen warlords invoke Islam in presidential race.

text.p: "There is no ruler save Allah", proclaims a brightly coloured election banner in Grozny's grey, war-wrecked city centre. "There is no power apart from His power, no law apart from His law."
The bullet and shell-scarred walls of still largely uninhabited buildings are plastered with campaign posters bearing slogans like "Islamic Order" and "God is Great".

Nearly five months after a peace deal halted bloody fighting between Russian troops and pro-independence guerrillas, breakaway Chechnya is in the grip of election fever and Islam is a key feature of the campaign.

All the main presidential candidates in the January 27 poll portray themselves as devout Moslems and have pledged to build an Islamic state if elected, though it is still not clear what this would entail in practice.

"We will build a Chechen Islamic state, taking into account the national traits and traditions of our people," Aslan Maskhadov, former chief commander of the rebel fighters and one of the front-runners for the presidency, told a rally.

Another candidate, former information minister Movladi Udugov, calls in his election leaflets for the creation of an Islamic bank and the prohibition of interest payments, in line with traditional religious teachings.
The two other main candidates, acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and guerrilla commander Shamil Basayev, are equally vocal in their espousal of Islamic values.
ISLAM IS POWERFUL WEAPON IN FIGHT AGAINST RUSSIANS
The presidential contenders, all staunch supporters of Chechen independence, begin and end their campaign rallies with the intonation "Allahu Akbar" (God is great).
On the hustings Islamic symbols like the crescent moon are as common as the breakaway state's green, red and white flag or its emblem of a black wolf.
The strong emphasis on Islamic values reflects a yearning for order after the 21-month war in which tens of thousands of people, mostly civilians, were killed and many more driven from their homes.
Observors said Islam was above all a system of self-defence for Chechens against Russia, which has struggled to control the turbulent Caucasian region since tsarist times.

"Islam has always provided a counter-identity against Russian colonialism," said Tim Guldimann of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which is helping to organise this month's election.

But he said Chechnya's recent fight against Russia was nationalistic, not religious, noting that the rebels rarely invoked the Koran or the concept of Jihad (holy war) and had sought both Western and Islamic support for their cause.
CHECHENS TRADITIONALLY RELAXED ABOUT RELIGION

Aslan Dukayev, a professor at Grozny University, said former independence leader Dzhokar Dudayev started using Islam in 1991 as an ideological tool against Moscow-imposed communism. Dudayev was killed by a Russian rocket attack last year.
"Now Islam has become a password into power for all the warlords seeking the presidency," Dukayev said.
Dukayev noted that both Dudayev and his would-be successor, Maskhadov, were educated in military academies in the atheist Soviet Union and had turned to Islam later in their careers.
He said Chechens were traditionally relaxed about religious issues.
"Many Chechens observe Moslem rites like Ramadan but Islam is not so strong as a foundation of everyday life," he said.

Even Imam Shamil, the great 19th century warrior who tried to forge the Caucasian tribes into a unified Islamic force against Russia, used to say the Chechens were not a very religious people, Dukayev said.
The presidential candidates show little interest in changing Dudayev's secular constitution and they do not talk of handing political power to the mullahs as in Iran.
SHARIAT LEGAL CODE IS KEY ISSUE OF ELECTION CAMPAIGN
Much of the debate about the role of Islam is focused on the Shariat, the traditional Islamic legal code that is strictly enforced in many Moslem countries.
The OSCE's Guldimann said the question of whether to introduce the Shariat would have to be tackled after the election, adding that the current situation was very confused.

Chechnya's legal system, like its political institutions, is in a state of limbo and the courts, like almost everything else in the devastated republic, are short of cash and function only haphazardly.
"There are no prisons to punish looters, for example. The authorites can hardly shoot them and they can't just let them go so offenders are given a beating instead," said Guldimann.
Technically Chechnya remains part of the Russian Federation and Russian laws are applicable.

Under the peace deal the region's final political status has been deferred for five years but the rebel leaders regard this as a face-saving formula for Moscow following its military humiliation. For them Chechen independence is a fait accompli.
Dukayev was sceptical about the chances of introducing the Shariat after the elections, saying Chechnya lacked the trained scholars and lawyers to make the system practicable.

"People are fed up with the disorder all around them, they think that introducing the Shariat will bring an immediate halt to crime, but fear of severe penalties is not going to deter the bandits," he said.
